about: Nine Tails Tales 편성표. 루틴은 `python gumiho/tales/tales.py next --date <오늘>` 이 준 한 편만 쓴다(날짜로 결정론적 배정). facts 는 확인된 뼈대, careful 은 단정하면 안 되는 것. format: tale(설화) · urban(현대 괴담) · list(카운트다운) · versus(대결) · behind(유명 작품 속 진짜 한국 — 작품은 입구, 이야기는 설화) · mystery(실제 기록·장소의 미스터리). ★2026-10-01 재편: 영어권 대형 공포 채널은 실화·실제 장소·인터넷 괴담이 주류이고, 옛 설화 '소개'는 채널 평균의 10~15%에 그친다 — 옛이야기는 4편에 1편 이하로 — 같은 틀이 연속되지 않게 섞는다. 지역: 한국이 기본, 3~4편마다 일본·중국(수요가 한국 주제의 5~50배 — 2026-09-29 조사). 10월(할로윈 달)은 가장 무서운 편을 앞에 둔다. ★2026-10-02 1주 형식 실험(sprint): 10/4~10/10 하루 한 편(3~9화), 10/14 부터 주 1편(10화~). pov = 2인칭(you) 이야기.

tales.title_idea: Korea's Nine-Tailed Fox Is Darker Than Japan's Kitsune
The Fox Sister: Korea's Most Terrifying Folk Tale
tales.angle: A family begs heaven for a daughter. They get one. Every night after, a cow dies with its liver missing.
facts: Korean folk tale 여우누이 (Yeou-nui, 'Fox Sister'), told in many regional versions
A rich family with several sons prays for a daughter; a girl is born (or arrives) and is doted on
Livestock start dying each night; a son is set to keep watch and sees the girl slip her arm into a cow and eat its liver
The father refuses to believe him and drives him out (other sons lie to please the father)
Years later he returns with three magic bottles (commonly white, red, blue) from a helper (a monk, a wife, or the Dragon King's daughter depending on version)
The village is empty; the fox sister has eaten everyone; she greets him sweetly and tries to eat him
He flees on horseback throwing the bottles: a thorn forest, a sea of fire, a sea of water — the fox drowns or burns
careful: Bottle colors and the helper differ by version — say 'in one version'
Keep the liver scenes implied, not graphic
tales.tie_in: Classic Korean horror; the 'three bottles' chase appears in many Asian magic-flight tales (compare Japan's Sanmai no ofuda)
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 여우누이: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: 7 Korean Superstitions That Could Get You Killed (or Worse)
tales.angle: In Korea, cutting your nails at night can let a mouse steal your whole life. Gumi counts down seven rules Koreans still half-believe.
facts: Fan death (선풍기 사망): the belief that sleeping in a closed room with an electric fan on can kill you; widely held in Korea since the late 20th century; fans were sold with timers; there is no scientific support — say so plainly
Red ink: writing a living person's name in red is taboo, because red was used for the names of the dead
The number 4 (사) sounds like the Sino-Korean word for death (死); many buildings label the 4th floor 'F' or skip it
Whistling at night is said to call snakes or ghosts

Folk tale 손톱 먹은 들쥐: a mouse eats a man's discarded nail clippings, turns into his exact double and takes over his home; the family can't tell them apart until a cat exposes the fake — hence 'don't cut your nails at night'
Eating seaweed soup (miyeokguk) before an exam means you'll 'slip' and fail
Giving shoes to a lover means they'll walk away from you
careful: These are beliefs, some half-joking today — don't mock them and don't claim they're true
Fan death: state clearly it has no scientific basis
tales.tie_in: Evergreen; very shareable with viewers aged 13–30 (countdown format)
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 손톱 먹은 들쥐, 금기어: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: The Real Korean Legends Hidden in KPop Demon Hunters
tales.angle: The Saja Boys' black hats weren't invented for a cartoon. In Korea, men in black have come for the dying for centuries — and families still set out rice for them.
facts: KPop Demon Hunters (2025) is an animated musical film by Sony Pictures Animation released on Netflix, directed by Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans. Premise: a K-pop girl group (Huntrix) secretly protects the world from demons with their voices

The rival boy band is the Saja Boys — 'saja' echoes jeoseung saja (저승사자), the envoys of the afterlife who escort the dead; their black robes and black gat hats match the modern pop image of the reaper
Saja-bap: at traditional funerals families set out rice, money and straw sandals for the reapers so they treat the soul kindly
Jeju shaman epic Chasa-bonpuri: the clever official Gangrim captures King Yeomra (ruler of the underworld) and becomes a reaper
The black gat and black robe look is largely a modern image popularized by TV and film (Guardian: The Lonely and Great God, 2016; Along with the Gods, 2017)

The tiger and magpie companions echo kkachi-horangi (까치호랑이, 'magpie and tiger'), a beloved Joseon-era folk painting (minhwa) genre: a goofy, harmless-looking tiger under a pine with a magpie; the magpie brings good news and the tiger wards off evil, and the tiger is often drawn comically

Mudang (무당) — Korean shamans, mostly women — perform gut (굿) rituals with song, dance, drums and bright costumes to call, appease or drive away spirits; this is the folk root for singers who protect people from spirits
careful: Talk about the film only through its premise and visible designs — no plot spoilers past the first act, no quotes from the film, no film characters or scenes in pictures (draw the folklore itself)
Say the film 'echoes' or 'draws on' a tradition unless a source says the creators stated it; never invent quotes from the directors
Don't claim the black-robe reaper costume is ancient
Respect shamanism as a living religion; don't mock mudang
Use the film title as text only; never imply this channel is affiliated with Netflix or Sony
tales.tie_in: KPop Demon Hunters became Netflix's most-watched film (Korea Herald, 2025-08-27) — strong search demand from viewers aged 13–34 for the Korean culture behind it
sources: Netflix Tudum — KPop Demon Hunters
Korea Herald (2025-08-27): KPop Demon Hunters becomes Netflix's most-watched film
Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 저승사자, 사자밥, 차사본풀이: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr
Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 까치호랑이(민화), 무당, 굿: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: Gumiho vs Kitsune vs Huli Jing: Which Nine-Tailed Fox Would Win?
tales.angle: Three nine-tailed foxes, three countries, one very biased judge.
facts: Korea's gumiho: almost always malevolent in folklore; human liver motif; fox bead (yeowoo guseul)
Japan's kitsune: messengers of the rice god Inari as well as tricksters; gain tails with age; famous villain Tamamo-no-Mae
China's huli jing: in early texts (Classic of Mountains and Seas) the nine-tailed fox is a man-eater, while in Han-era thought it could be an auspicious omen; Daji in Investiture of the Gods
Rounds: origins, powers (shapeshifting, possession, fox fire), weaknesses (dogs, being discovered, losing the bead), most famous case, pop culture
careful: Gumi is openly biased toward the gumiho — play it as a joke
Don't overlap episode 1's fox bead story beyond one line
tales.tie_in: Linfamy's comparison video passed 300K views
sources: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas)
Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 구미호
Otogizoshi — Tamamo-no-Mae

tales.title_idea: The Elevator Game: The Korean Ritual That Takes You to Another World
tales.angle: Ride an elevator alone. Press 4, 2, 6, 2, 10, then 5. If a woman gets on at the fifth floor — don't look at her, and don't say a word.
facts: The Elevator Game is an internet ritual: alone in an elevator of a building with at least 10 floors, you press the floors in a fixed order (commonly 4, 2, 6, 2, 10, then 5); a woman may get on at floor 5 and you must not speak to or look at her; if it 'works', pressing 1 takes you up instead of down, to an 'other world'
Common details of the 'other world': the building looks the same but you are the only person, the lights are off, and in some versions a red cross glows in the distance
It is usually said to have started on Korean internet forums and spread to English-language sites in the 2010s
It belongs to a family of 'ritual' creepypastas where following steps exactly is the scary part
careful: It's an internet legend — say 'is said to', never claim anyone was taken
Do NOT mention or link any real person's death or real criminal case to the game
Don't encourage viewers to try it in a real building (no instructions framed as a dare); Gumi can joke that she wouldn't
The Korean origin is commonly claimed but not proven — say so
tales.tie_in: One of the best-known internet rituals in English creepypasta culture — the Korean origin is the hook
sources: Wikipedia — Elevator game
Creepypasta wiki / Know Your Meme — Elevator Game (origin claims)

tales.title_idea: In 2022, a Stone in Japan Split in Half — and a Nine-Tailed Fox Walked Free
tales.angle: In March 2022 hikers found the Killing Stone at Nasu cracked in two. The internet asked: what was sealed inside?
facts: Sessho-seki (the Killing Stone) at Nasu, Tochigi was found split in March 2022 (widely reported)
Legend: Tamamo-no-Mae, a beautiful and brilliant courtesan of Emperor Toba (12th century), made him ill; the onmyoji Abe no Yasunari exposed her as a nine-tailed fox
She fled to Nasu, was killed by warriors (Miura-no-suke, Kazusa-no-suke), and her spirit became a poison stone that killed anything that touched it
Later tellings link her to China's Daji and an Indian queen — the same fox across three empires
Kitsune in Japan are also Inari's messengers — foxes aren't always villains there
careful: The stone likely split from weathering — say that plainly
Gumi calls kitsune her 'cousins'
tales.tie_in: Naruto's Nine-Tails and countless anime borrow from Tamamo
sources: Nasu town / Tochigi tourism pages on Sessho-seki
Otogizoshi & Noh play 'Sessho-seki'

tales.title_idea: In 1609, Korea's Royal Records Logged Something Burning in the Sky
tales.angle: Joseon officials didn't believe in flying saucers. But in 1609, five towns sent the king the same report: something round and burning, crossing the sky.
facts: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (Gwanghaegun Ilgi, 1609) record reports from Gangwon Province of bright objects seen in the sky in several towns (including Yangyang and Gangneung) on the same day
Witnesses described shapes like a round vessel or a bright disc with fire, moving and making sounds
The record is often cited by modern UFO enthusiasts as Korea's oldest UFO report
Joseon courts recorded unusual sky phenomena carefully because they were read as omens about the king's rule
careful: It's a real historical record of something unexplained — don't claim aliens; mention natural explanations (bright meteor/fireball) as the likely reading
Quote only what the record says in paraphrase; don't invent exact wording or witness names
Keep dates as given by sources (1609, Gwanghaegun's first year)
tales.tie_in: Real-record mysteries travel well in English ('the royal court wrote it down')
sources: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty — Gwanghaegun Ilgi, 1609 (sillok.history.go.kr)
Korea JoongAng Daily / Korea Times features on the 1609 Gangwon sky record

tales.title_idea: The Tiger of Mount Jang Can Speak in Your Mother's Voice
tales.angle: YOU are the one on the trail. Second person, present tense: you hike Mount Jang alone at dusk, you hear your mother call your name from the trees — but your mother is at home. Gumi interrupts at the turning points to tell you what the legend says happens next.
facts: Jangsanbeom (장산범) is a 21st-century Korean internet legend from Jangsan mountain in Busan
Described as a pale, long-haired creature that moves on all fours and mimics human voices
It inherits older Korean tiger lore — in folk tales tigers imitate human voices, e.g., the tiger that disguises itself as the mother in 'The Sun and the Moon' (해와 달이 된 오누이)
Film The Mimic (2017) is based on it
careful: It's a modern legend — say so; don't present sightings as fact
tales.tie_in: Korean creepypasta; Beauties & Beasts' Jangsanbeom video passed 300K views
sources: Film The Mimic (장산범, 2017)
Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 해와 달이 된 오누이

tales.title_idea: Gonjiam: The Real Korean Asylum Called One of the Creepiest Places on Earth
tales.angle: In 2012 CNN listed an abandoned hospital in the Korean hills among the freakiest places on the planet. The rumors about what happened inside were worse than the truth.
facts: Gonjiam Psychiatric Hospital (곤지암 정신병원) was an abandoned hospital building near Gonjiam in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province
Rumors claimed patients died there and that the director vanished; reports say the hospital simply closed in the 1990s and the rumors of mass deaths are not supported
CNN Travel (2012) listed it among 'seven of the freakiest places on the planet'
The found-footage horror film Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum (2018) was a box-office hit in Korea
The building was demolished in 2018
careful: Separate rumor from fact clearly — the scary stories are rumors; don't present them as events
It was private property and trespassing was illegal; don't encourage urbex
No real former patients, staff or owners named or depicted
Mental illness: never mock patients; the horror is the rumor machine, not the people
tales.tie_in: Real-place horror ('What Happened Here…') is the strongest English horror pattern (Scary Interesting 1.47M for a real Japanese island)
sources: CNN Travel (2012): 7 of the freakiest places on the planet
Coverage of the film Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum (2018) and the building's 2018 demolition (Korea Herald / Korea JoongAng Daily)

tales.title_idea: Dokkaebi: Korea's Goblins Want to Wrestle You, Not Eat You
tales.angle: Meet a dokkaebi on a dark road and he won't kill you. He'll challenge you to wrestle till dawn.
facts: Dokkaebi (도깨비) are Korean goblin spirits, often born from old household objects (a broom, a pestle) touched by human blood
Love ssireum (wrestling), buckwheat jelly (memil-muk) and practical jokes; can be dim-witted and are often outsmarted
Dokkaebi bangmangi — a magic club that produces anything when struck ('gold, come out!')
Folk tale 혹부리 영감 (The Old Man with the Lump): a kind old man sings, goblins buy his lump thinking it's where the song lives; a greedy neighbor tries the same and gets a second lump
Dokkaebi-bul: ghostly will-o'-the-wisp lights
careful: Horned red oni-style dokkaebi is a 20th-century image influenced by Japanese oni — say so
Not demons
tales.tie_in: K-drama Guardian: The Lonely and Great God (Goblin, 2016); KPop Demon Hunters' tiger-and-magpie art comes from the same folk-painting world
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 도깨비, 혹부리 영감: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: The Real Korean Shamans and Grave Curses Behind Exhuma
tales.angle: In Korea, when a family's luck keeps going wrong, someone eventually asks the question Exhuma starts with: is it the grave?
facts: Exhuma (파묘, 2024) is a Korean occult thriller directed by Jang Jae-hyun; premise: a shaman, her apprentice, a geomancer and an undertaker are hired to move a wealthy family's ancestral grave. It drew over 10 million cinema admissions in Korea
Pungsu-jiri (풍수지리, Korean geomancy): the belief that where an ancestor is buried affects the fortunes of the descendants; families consult a geomancer (jigwan, 지관) to choose a grave site
Ijang (이장) — moving a grave — is done with rituals and care; opening a grave (pamyo) is treated as serious and dangerous to the family's luck
Mudang (무당) — Korean shamans, mostly women, mediating between people and spirits; mansin is an honorific; spirit sickness (sinbyeong) often precedes initiation
Gut (굿) — shamanic rituals with music, costume changes and possession; e.g., jakdu-tagi (작두타기), where the shaman dances barefoot on straw-cutter blades as a sign the spirit has come
Many shrines on Mount Inwang in Seoul (Guksadang)
careful: Premise only — never reveal the film's second-half twist or ending
If you mention the story of iron stakes driven into Korean mountains (쇠말뚝), present it as a widely told belief that historians dispute, not as fact
Be respectful — shamanism is a living religious practice
No film characters or scenes in pictures; draw graves, shrines, rituals, mountains
tales.tie_in: Exhuma (2024) was one of Korea's biggest hits and reached global streaming; evergreen search for 'Korean shaman' and 'pamyo'
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 무당, 굿, 작두타기, 풍수, 이장: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr
Laurel Kendall, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (1985)
Korea JoongAng Daily / Yonhap coverage of Exhuma's box office (2024)

tales.title_idea: 'Am I Pretty?' — The Slit-Mouthed Woman Who Crossed the Sea to Korea
tales.angle: A woman in a surgical mask stops a child walking home and asks one question. Every answer is wrong.
facts: Kuchisake-onna (口裂け女, 'slit-mouthed woman') is a Japanese urban legend; a panic spread among Japanese schoolchildren in 1979, and some schools had children walk home in groups
She wears a mask and asks 'Am I pretty?'; unmasked, her mouth is cut from ear to ear; 'no' and 'yes' both end badly
Escape tricks in the rumors: answer 'you're average', throw candy (bekko-ame) at her, or say 'pomade' three times
Some claim much older roots in Edo-period tales — the evidence is thin
In Korea she became 'Ppalgan Mask' (빨간 마스크, the Red Mask), a rumor that swept elementary schools in the 2000s
careful: Modern legend — present sightings as rumors
Keep the mouth imagery implied (mask, shadow), no gore
tales.tie_in: Japanese urban legend videos regularly pass 1M views
sources: Michael Dylan Foster, 'The Question of the Slit-Mouthed Woman' (Asian Folklore Studies, 2007)

tales.title_idea: Bunshinsaba: The Spirit Game Korean Students Were Told Never to Play
tales.angle: Two students hold one pen. They whisper a chant they don't understand. The pen starts to move — and it won't stop.
facts: Bunshinsaba (분신사바) is a spirit-summoning game played by Korean students: two people hold one pen over paper and chant 'bunshinsaba, bunshinsaba, oide kudasai', then ask questions as the pen moves
It descends from the Japanese game kokkuri-san (a ouija-like table game); the chant mixes Japanese words
Schools and parents warned students against it; stories say you must end the session properly or the spirit stays
The horror film Bunshinsaba (2004) made the game famous across Korea
careful: Folk belief and school rumor — don't claim spirits are real
No instructions framed as a dare; don't encourage children to play
tales.tie_in: Bridges to the known ouija board and Japan's kokkuri-san
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 분신사바 / 학교 괴담: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr
Film Bunshinsaba (분신사바, 2004)

tales.title_idea: Every Magistrate Who Slept in This Town Died by Morning
tales.angle: In Miryang, every new magistrate was found dead the morning after he arrived. Then one of them stayed awake.
facts: Arang legend of Miryang (밀양 아랑 전설): the magistrate's daughter Arang (often named Yun Jeong-ok) is murdered after refusing a servant's advances
Her ghost appears to each new magistrate, who dies of fright
A brave new magistrate (often Yi Sang-sa) listens; she tells him her killer; the body is found and justice done; her ghost is at peace
The Arang shrine (Arang-gak) stands near Yeongnamnu pavilion in Miryang
Arang is the model of the cheonyeo gwishin — the young woman's ghost with long black hair and white clothes, driven by han (unresolved grief)
careful: Names differ between versions
No graphic violence
tales.tie_in: K-drama Arang and the Magistrate (2012); the long-haired ghost look later seen in J-horror
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 아랑전설: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr
Miryang city tourism — Arang-gak

tales.title_idea: At Midnight, Korea's School Statues Come Alive
tales.angle: Every Korean kid knows it: at midnight, Admiral Yi draws his sword and King Sejong turns a page.
facts: Hakgyo goedam (학교 괴담, school ghost stories) are a staple of Korean childhood

Common versions: the Admiral Yi Sun-sin statue draws its sword or walks at midnight; the King Sejong statue turns the page of its book; the anatomy model in the science room walks; the eyes of the Beethoven portrait in the music room follow you; a 13th stair or an extra floor appears at night
The film Whispering Corridors (여고괴담, 1998) launched a long-running school-horror franchise
Similar school legends exist in Japan (gakkō no kaidan, e.g., Hanako-san of the toilet)
careful: Present as rumors kids trade; no real schools or real students named
tales.tie_in: Nostalgic for Korean viewers, fresh for global ones; Japan comparison adds reach
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 학교괴담: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr
Film Whispering Corridors (1998)

tales.title_idea: 7 Korean Ghosts You Should Never Meet After Dark
tales.angle: A ghost with no face at all. A drowned ghost that pulls swimmers down. Korea has a ghost for every kind of bad night.
facts: Cheonyeo gwishin — unmarried young woman's ghost (white clothes, long hair), driven by han
Mongdal gwishin — ghost of a man who died unmarried
Mul gwishin — water ghosts that drag swimmers down
Dalgyal gwishin — 'egg ghost', a ghost with a completely blank, featureless face
Gaksi — bride ghosts; Songaksi — ghost of a young woman who died unmarried, a household spirit in some regions
Jibakryeong-style 'bound' ghosts are a modern borrowing — note it if used
careful: Dalgyal gwishin is mostly modern/urban-legend — say so
List format but each with a mini story
tales.tie_in: Netflix The East Palace (2026)
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 처녀귀신, 몽달귀신, 물귀신: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: Two Sisters Came Back From the Dead to Name Their Killer
tales.angle: Two sisters die in the same pond. Every magistrate they visit dies of fright. The third one listens.
facts: Janghwa Hongryeon jeon (장화홍련전), Joseon-era tale based on a Pyeongan-do case
A stepmother frames the elder sister Janghwa with a fake miscarriage (a skinned rat) to shame her; Janghwa is drowned in a pond; younger sister Hongryeon follows her
Their ghosts appear to magistrates who die of fright until magistrate Jeong Dong-u listens and exposes the stepmother
In the ending the sisters are reborn as twins to their father
careful: Keep the 'skinned rat' mention brief and non-graphic
tales.tie_in: Film A Tale of Two Sisters (2003), remade in Hollywood as The Uninvited (2009)
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture — 장화홍련전: https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr

tales.title_idea: 5 Korean Monsters Nobody Outside Korea Knows About
tales.angle: Dogs that bite the sun. A serpent that waits a thousand years to become a dragon. Korea's bestiary is stranger than you think.
facts: Bulgae (불개): fire dogs sent from a dark kingdom (Gamangnara) to steal the sun and moon; their bites are why eclipses happen
Imugi (이무기): a great serpent that must endure a thousand years (or win a magic pearl, yeouiju) to become a dragon; one that fails turns bitter and dangerous (film D-War, 2007)
Haetae (해태): a lion-like guardian said to devour fire; statues stand before Gyeongbokgung palace; today Seoul's mascot is based on it
Samjok-o (삼족오): the three-legged crow of the sun, painted in Goguryeo tomb murals
Eop-gureongi (업구렁이): a great serpent that lives under a house as its luck spirit — harm it and the family's fortune leaves
careful: Versions vary; the fire-eating haetae story around Gyeongbokgung is tradition, not proven history
tales.tie_in: Imugi appears in K-dramas (e.g., Tale of the Nine Tailed)
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 불개, 이무기, 해태, 삼족오, 업: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: The Fox Who Ended a Dynasty: Daji and the Fall of Shang
tales.angle: Three thousand years ago a king fell in love with the most beautiful woman in China. She wasn't a woman.
facts: Daji, consort of King Zhou, last king of Shang (c. 11th century BCE) — historical figure turned legend
In the Ming novel Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi) a thousand-year-old fox spirit possesses her on the goddess Nüwa's orders
Legendary cruelties: the Paolao bronze pillar, the pool of wine and forest of meat
Jiang Ziya and King Wu of Zhou overthrow Shang; the fox is executed
Japanese legend later says the same fox fled to become Tamamo-no-Mae
careful: Separate history from the novel
Torture mentioned, not shown
tales.tie_in: Chinese film Creation of the Gods I (2023); Tamamo episode #5
sources: Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods)
Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian — Annals of Yin

tales.title_idea: The Princess Her Father Threw Away Became the Goddess of the Dead
tales.angle: A king ordered his seventh daughter thrown into the sea at birth. Years later, only she could save his life.
facts: Bari Gongju / Barideogi (바리공주) — shaman epic sung at Korean rites for the dead
The king, wanting a son, abandons his seventh daughter in a jade box on the water; she's raised by an old couple
The king falls deathly ill; only medicinal water from the otherworld can cure him; none of the six elder daughters will go
Bari travels to the underworld, serves its guardian (Mujangseung) for years, marries him and bears sons, returns with the water and flowers of life
She revives her parents and becomes the goddess who guides the dead — patron of Korean shamans (mudang)
careful: Many versions — number of sons and tasks vary
tales.tie_in: The shaman lineage behind KPop Demon Hunters' heroines
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 바리공주: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr

tales.title_idea: Korea's Grim Reaper vs Japan's Shinigami vs China's Ox-Head and Horse-Face
tales.angle: Three countries, three ways to be collected when you die. Which one would you rather meet?
facts: Korea: jeoseung saja escort the dead, often in threes, carrying a register of names; families offer saja-bap (rice, sandals, coins)
China: Ox-Head and Horse-Face (牛頭馬面) are guardians/escorts of the underworld (Diyu) under King Yama; also Heibai Wuchang, the black and white guards of impermanence
Japan: 'shinigami' as a death god is largely a later concept (Edo-period tales and rakugo like 'Shinigami'), popularized worldwide by manga such as Death Note
Rounds: who they are, how they find you, can you bribe or trick them, the afterlife they take you to
careful: Say plainly that shinigami is a comparatively recent idea
Keep Buddhist/Taoist beliefs respectful
tales.tie_in: Follows the jeoseung saja episode; Death Note and Bleach fans
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 저승사자
Rakugo 'Shinigami' (San'yūtei Enchō, Meiji era)

tales.title_idea: The Snow Woman Spared Him — on One Condition
tales.angle: In a blizzard, a woman made of snow killed an old woodcutter and let the young one live. If he ever told anyone...
facts: Lafcadio Hearn's 'Yuki-Onna' in Kwaidan (1904): woodcutters Mosaku and Minokichi shelter from a blizzard
Yuki-onna freezes Mosaku with her breath, spares Minokichi on condition he never tells
He marries a beautiful woman, O-Yuki; they have ten children; she never ages
Years later he tells her the story; she reveals she is the snow woman, spares him for the children's sake, and melts away
careful: Hearn's version is the famous one; older regional yuki-onna tales differ
tales.tie_in: Countless anime; Kwaidan film (1964)
sources: Lafcadio Hearn, Kwaidan (1904) — public domain

tales.title_idea: The Monster That Ate Iron — and the Dictator Who Kidnapped a Director to Film It
tales.angle: A Korean legend about a monster that couldn't be killed. A North Korean remake that required kidnapping South Korea's greatest director.
facts: Bulgasari (불가살이) legend of late Goryeo: a creature formed from rice (in many versions by a monk) that eats iron and grows; 'bulgasari' puns on 'cannot be killed'
It ate the country's iron — needles, spoons, weapons — and could not be killed by blades; fire in some versions
Real history: director Shin Sang-ok and actress Choi Eun-hee were abducted to North Korea in 1978 on Kim Jong-il's orders
Shin directed the monster film Pulgasari (1985) there; the couple escaped at the US embassy in Vienna in 1986
careful: Legend ending varies
Keep the politics factual and short — this is a tale channel
tales.tie_in: Pulgasari (1985), often compared to Godzilla
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 불가살이
Paul Fischer, A Kim Jong-Il Production (2015)

tales.title_idea: Why Chinese Vampires Hop
tales.angle: In old China, corpses walked home in single file at night, hopping — and a priest with a bell led the way.
facts: Jiangshi (僵尸) — 'stiff corpse', a reanimated body that drains qi from the living
Linked to the 'corpse herders' of Xiangxi, Hunan, said to guide the dead home for burial at night
Remedies in folklore: Taoist talismans on the forehead, holding your breath, mirrors, sticky rice, peach wood
Mr. Vampire (1985, Hong Kong) made the hopping vampire iconic
careful: Corpse-herding practicalities are debated — say 'according to legend'
tales.tie_in: Hong Kong horror-comedy classics; Genshin Impact's Qiqi
sources: Yuan Mei, Zi Bu Yu (18th c.) — jiangshi tales
Mr. Vampire (1985)

tales.title_idea: Korea's Grim Reapers Don't Carry Scythes — They Carry a List
tales.angle: When a Korean family lays out three bowls of rice and straw sandals at a funeral, it isn't for the dead. It's for the ones who came to collect them.
facts: Jeoseung saja (저승사자) = messenger/envoy of the afterlife (jeoseung) who escorts the dead
Saja-bap: at traditional funerals families set out rice, money and straw sandals for the reapers so they treat the soul kindly
Jeju shaman epic Chasa-bonpuri: the clever official Gangrim captures King Yeomra (ruler of the underworld) and becomes a reaper
Often described as coming in threes in shamanic tradition
The black gat and black robe look is largely a modern image popularized by TV and film (e.g., Guardian: The Lonely and Great God, 2016; Along with the Gods, 2017)
careful: Don't claim the black-robe costume is ancient
Details of Chasa-bonpuri vary; keep the core: Gangrim, Yeomra, becoming a reaper
tales.tie_in: Deep dive after the KPop Demon Hunters episode (tale 4) — the full Chasa-bonpuri story of how a man became a reaper
sources: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture — 저승사자, 사자상, 차사본풀이: https://folkency.nfm.go.kr
